tests.title: Vehicle.java compiles with plain javac, no warnings, output lands in the declared package path
tests.rationale: The repo has no build file, so javac is the only critical-path check. It proves the file exists, compiles on the JDK alone (no Maven/Lombok), produces no warnings, and the class file is written to com/neversoft/vehicle, which confirms the package matches the directory. A lower layer cannot prove this because it is a property of the whole file as compiled.
traces_to: risk: No build tooling to verify compilation in CI
risk: "Mojo" actually means a Maven plugin Mojo

tests.title: Change set only adds Vehicle.java; no tracked file is modified
tests.rationale: AC-6 is a repository-level property, not code behaviour, so only a git check can prove it. Expect exactly one 'A' entry for src/main/java/com/neversoft/vehicle/Vehicle.java (plus docs/bob/1/ and any approved test files) and no 'M' or 'D' entries.

tests.title: Developer can load Vehicle by its fully qualified name
tests.gherkin:
Given Vehicle.java has been compiled with javac
When a developer loads the class com.neversoft.vehicle.Vehicle
Then the class is found
And it is declared public
And its package is com.neversoft.vehicle
tests.target: src/test/java/com/neversoft/vehicle/VehicleTest.java (scenario method, plain JDK main-method harness, no JUnit)
tests.rationale: Shows the AC-1 location/package contract from the consumer's side: the class is reachable at the expected name. It needs the compiled class, so it sits above unit level, but it is cheap to run in the same harness as the other scenarios.

tests.title: Developer builds a Vehicle with the no-arg constructor and fills it in with setters
tests.gherkin:
Given a new Vehicle created with the no-arg constructor
When the developer sets id 42, make "Ford", model "Focus", year 2019, vin "WF0AXXGCDA1A12345", color "blue" and mileage 55000
Then getId returns 42, getMake returns "Ford", getModel returns "Focus", getYear returns 2019
And getVin returns "WF0AXXGCDA1A12345", getColor returns "blue" and getMileage returns 55000
tests.rationale: Acceptance-level walk through the JavaBean usage a caller will actually perform (no-arg constructor plus setters plus getters). Per-field and edge behaviour is pushed down to T-9 and T-11.

tests.title: Developer builds a Vehicle with the all-fields constructor
tests.gherkin:
Given the values id 7, make "Toyota", model "Corolla", year 2021, vin "JTDKB20U777123456", color "red", mileage 1200
When the developer calls new Vehicle(7, "Toyota", "Corolla", 2021, "JTDKB20U777123456", "red", 1200)
Then every getter returns the value supplied for that field
tests.rationale: Caller-visible proof of the all-fields constructor contract. Argument-order mistakes are caught precisely at unit level in T-10.

tests.title: Two vehicles with the same data are equal and print all their fields
tests.gherkin:
Given two Vehicle objects created with identical field values
When the developer compares them with equals and reads their hashCode
Then equals returns true and the hash codes are identical
And changing the vin on one makes equals return false
And toString of a vehicle mentions every field value
tests.rationale: AC-4 is a user-visible value-object contract (e.g. use in collections, logging). One end-to-end scenario shows it; branch coverage lives in T-12 to T-16.

tests.title: Vehicle declares exactly seven private instance fields with the specified types
tests.rationale: Field names, types (long id, String make, String model, int year, String vin, String color, long mileage) and private visibility are structural facts best checked by reflection. No higher layer needed. The test is deliberately tied to the provisional field list, so it must be updated when fields change.
traces_to: risk: Field set does not match the author's needs

tests.title: Vehicle is a plain POJO: extends Object, implements no interfaces, no Maven Mojo types
tests.rationale: Guards the POJO interpretation of 'mojo'. A Maven Mojo would extend AbstractMojo and need Maven dependencies, so this fails fast if the class drifts into that shape. The remaining half of the risk (author really meant a Maven Mojo) is a human confirmation, see gaps.
traces_to: risk: "Mojo" actually means a Maven plugin Mojo

tests.title: No-arg constructor is public and leaves primitives at 0 and Strings at null
tests.rationale: Pure constructor logic. Verifies the documented default state (id 0, year 0, mileage 0, make/model/vin/color null) and that the constructor is public.

tests.title: All-fields constructor assigns each argument to the matching field using seven distinct values
tests.rationale: Uses seven different values (and two different Strings for make/model/vin/color) so transposed arguments, such as make and model swapped, fail. Also checks that no validation is applied (empty strings, negative numbers and nulls are stored as given).

tests.title: Every getter returns what its setter stored, including null and boundary values
tests.rationale: Seven setter/getter pairs with JavaBean names. Includes null for each String, Long.MAX_VALUE for id and mileage, and Integer.MAX_VALUE/0 for year. Also checks that setting one field leaves the others unchanged, which catches a setter assigning the wrong field.

tests.title: equals honours its contract: reflexive, symmetric, null, other type, equal copies
tests.rationale: Covers each early branch of equals (identity, null, getClass mismatch) and the equal-copy case. Pure logic in one class.

tests.title: equals returns false when any single one of the seven fields differs
tests.target: src/test/java/com/neversoft/vehicle/VehicleTest.java (loop over seven mutations of a baseline)
tests.rationale: Proves equals covers all fields, not a subset. This is the main defect risk for a hand-written equals, and it needs one mutation per field.

tests.title: equals, hashCode and toString do not throw with null String fields
tests.rationale: The LLP promises null safety through Objects.equals and Objects.hash. Checks two default (all-null) vehicles are equal with equal hashes, a null-String vehicle differs from a populated one in both directions, and toString returns a non-null string.

tests.title: hashCode is consistent with equals and stable across calls
tests.rationale: Equal objects must have equal hash codes, and repeated calls on an unmodified object must return the same value. Also checks that mutating a field and restoring it returns the original hash. Single-class logic.

tests.title: toString includes the value of all seven fields
tests.rationale: Builds a vehicle with seven recognisable values and asserts each appears in the output, so a field omitted from toString is caught. The exact format is deliberately not asserted because it is not part of the requirement.

gaps: No component tests: Vehicle is a single standalone class with no API, event, database or module boundary, and nothing else references it.
AC-5 and AC-6 have smoke coverage only (T-1, T-2). They are build and repository properties, not behaviours, so BDD scenarios would add nothing.
Risk 'Mojo actually means a Maven plugin Mojo' is only partly guarded (T-1, T-8). Confirming the interpretation with the author is a human step recorded in the PR description.
Risk 'Chosen package name/location conflicts with later project structure' is not tested. It cannot be proven by a test, and moving a single file is trivial.

The test harness (src/test/java/com/neversoft/vehicle/VehicleTest.java) is not covered by the LLP, which lists only Vehicle.java and says the optional jshell check is not committed. No JUnit or build file exists, and adding them is out of scope. The plan therefore uses a dependency-free main-method harness run with javac and java. If the team prefers no extra file, T-3 to T-16 can be run as a throwaway jshell or java script instead. Either way T-2 must allow the added test file.
Exact toString format, input validation, thread safety and serialization are not tested, because the design specifies none of them.
